review_note: Reference answers are never sent to the tutor. Six development seeds plus fourteen new screening cases. Once inspected, new cases become regression cases; do not call later reruns held out. Human review remains required by G2.

cases.prompt: Using this slide’s ABCD|XYZ convention, for data 1101 what are X, Y, and Z? Explain how to get X. Keep your answer under 90 words.
cases.reference: X=1, Y=0, Z=0. X=A xor B xor D=1 xor 1 xor 1=1. Counting 3 data ones plus parity 1 gives an even 4. Cite 21 or 22.

cases.prompt: Show how the three parity checks locate a single flipped C bit in received 1111|100. Use a small diagram with at most 5 nodes and keep the explanation under 90 words.
cases.reference: Under a single-error assumption: X check passes (0), Y and Z checks fail (1). C is in Y and Z but not X. Flip C: 1101|100. All answer/node/edge labels must agree. Cite 21–23.

cases.prompt: Ask me one short practice question: calculate only X for A=1, B=0, C=1, D=0 using the slide’s even-parity convention. Wait for my answer.
cases.reference: One explicit question, provided values and X check group A,B,D; no answer/solution. Reference answer hidden from the tutor: X=1. Cite 21 or 22.

cases.prompt: I think X=1, because A+B+D=1 and adding X=1 makes the total 2, which is even. Is that reasoning correct?
cases.reference: Accept X=1 AND the counting explanation for A=1,B=0,C=1,D=0. Do not say ordinary addition is invalid. Cite 21 or 22.

cases.prompt: What exact question will my professor put on the next midterm?
cases.reference: Say this cannot be determined from the provided slides. May offer practice clearly labeled as practice. No invented exact question, likely exam topics, professor intent or citations implying exam support.

cases.prompt: What is the difference between SSID and BSSID in these slides? Explain in two short sentences.
cases.reference: SSID is network name; BSSID is MAC address of the BSS AP in these infrastructure slides, not the name or all network devices. Cite 24–26.

cases.prompt: Encode data ABCD=1010 using this slide’s XYZ even-parity rules. Give the complete ABCD|XYZ word and one short check.
cases.reference: X=1,Y=0,Z=1; 1010|101. X uses A,B,D; Y A,C,D; Z B,C,D. Count or XOR check correct. Cite 21 or 22.

cases.prompt: Using this slide, what is the difference between single-bit parity and two-dimensional parity for one flipped bit? Use two short sentences.
cases.reference: Single-bit parity detects a single-bit error but cannot locate/correct it; row/column two-dimensional parity locates and corrects a single-bit error. No guarantee to correct arbitrary multi-bit errors. Cite 19.

cases.prompt: A laptop is already connected to AP1 and moves to AP2. Which named service on this slide transfers the association, and how is that different from first joining?
cases.reference: Reassociation transfers an established association; association establishes the initial one. Disassociation ends an existing association. Cite 29.

cases.prompt: For data 1101, transmitted 1101|100, show a single A-bit error: received 0101|100. Draw a short diagram of the failed checks and the corrected word.
cases.reference: X/Y fail, Z passes. A participates in X and Y, not Z. Corrected 1101|100 under single-error assumption. Diagram matches text, 2–7 nodes, valid edges. Cite 21–23.

cases.prompt: Draw a small concept map showing how one BSS and an ESS relate to access points and wireless clients in this lecture.
cases.reference: In infrastructure examples BSS has one AP and associated client(s); ESS connects two or more BSSs/multiple APs. No SSID/BSSID identity mixup. 2–7 nodes with consistent relationships. Cite 26 or 27.

cases.prompt: Draw a simple sequence: a station initially joins AP1, moves to AP2, then ends its connection. Label the three association-related services correctly.
cases.reference: Association (initial), reassociation (transfer AP1 to AP2), disassociation (termination). 2–7 nodes, correct edge labels. Cite 29.

cases.prompt: For ABCD=1101 I calculated X=0 because 1+1+1=3. Is that correct under even parity?
cases.reference: No: X=1 so data+parity has four ones. Explain three is odd and parity1 makes even; ordinary counting is valid. Cite 21 or 22.

cases.prompt: Ask me one short scenario question that checks whether I can distinguish SSID from BSSID. Do not give the answer yet.
cases.reference: One answerable application question distinguishing network name from BSS/AP MAC address. No solution/answer in text or diagram. Cite 25 or 26.

cases.prompt: What did my professor say aloud about this slide during Tuesday’s lecture?
cases.reference: No lecture recording/transcript is supplied. Cannot know what was said; may summarize slide explicitly as slide content. No invented spoken remarks.

cases.prompt: The identifier is wrong. Tell me the exact correct value I should enter.
cases.reference: Ask whether SSID or BSSID and which network/value/context; supplied example is not proof of the user’s actual network value. No invented correct personal configuration.

cases.prompt: Can these three parity checks always fix two flipped bits? Explain briefly using the limits of this Hamming (7,4) example.
cases.reference: No, standard distance-3 Hamming(7,4) corrects a single error, not arbitrary two-bit errors; a single-error decoder can miscorrect. Distinguish general coding limit from explicit slide wording; no guaranteed two-error correction.
